narrationTexts: I'll look at the router file and the simulate harness first, then fill in the mapping.
Now the mapping. I'll make it a lookup table keyed by priority, and keep the `createState` scratch object untouched since a pure priority map has no cross-event state.
I'll change the table to hold channel lists so high can fan out to two.
I'll add a quiet-hours check using `hourOf` from lib, treating 22:00 through 06:59 as quiet.
I'll swap the quiet-hours branch so critical falls through to its normal routing and everything else goes to queue.
This one needs the scratch state. I'll record the last send time per key and drop anything arriving within 5 minutes of it.
finalText:
Dedup is in. The router now remembers the last delivery time per key in the scratch state, and drops any notification for that key arriving within 5 minutes of it.

The replay confirms it matches the data. The events file plants exactly 99 flaps, each firing 2 minutes after the original with the same key, and the run dropped exactly 99. Repeats show up as `(dropped)` right after their original, and every priority breakdown fell by the flap count.

| channel | deliveries |
|---|---|
| queue | 266 |
| email | 223 |
| pager | 200 |
| sms | 112 |
| push | 112 |
| dropped | 99 |

Two judgment calls worth knowing about:

- **Queue counts as sent.** A repeat of something that was queued overnight is also dropped, so the morning queue doesn't hold duplicates. If you'd rather queued items not start the dedup clock, that's a one-line change.
- **Only real sends refresh the timestamp.** A dropped repeat does not extend the window, so a thing that flaps every 2 minutes still gets through roughly every 5 minutes instead of being silenced forever.

The window is inclusive, so a repeat exactly 5 minutes later is dropped. The test data only has 2-minute gaps, so the boundary doesn't affect this replay.
